https://www.itv.com/news/central/2025-07.title: Birmingham street a 'dumping ground' littered with fridges and furniture amid rise in fly-tipping
https://www.itv.com/news/central/2025-07.text:
Fridges, furniture, toys and a shopping trolley are among items being dumped on a street in Birmingham, amid a rise in fly-tipping incidents across the city in recent months.
A resident has told ITV News Central their street in Ward End has become a "dumping ground" for fly-tipping over the past two months, with a smell of rotting food coming from bags of rubbish.
The resident, who has asked to remain anonymous, said they are now concerned the rubbish is causing a health and safety risk as it's not been collected by the council.
A section of Northleigh Road has been littered with all manner of waste including three fridge freezers, wooden furniture, black bags, a shopping trolley and children's toys.
Medication and tablets including paracetamol and allergy tablets can also been seen on the pavement.
The resident told ITV News Central: "It is now becoming a serious health and safety risk especially with medication on the floor, and fridge freezers standing upright which could topple over at any moment injuring people.
"I can also smell rotting food and see maggots amongst the rubbish."
They added: "Imagine if a child picked up the tablets and swallowed them, or of the 6 foot tall fridge freezers fell onto a person."
"Unfortunately this area of Ward End has become one huge rubbish tip, and the Council have given up on this area."
The resident says they have contacted the council over the past few weeks, but has not heard back from them.
Another resident, who asked not to be named, said: "It's really bad. More and more stuff just keeps appearing there.
"We've had problems in the past, but before the bin strikes it usually got picked up quite quickly. That's just not happening now.
"This is the worst I've seen it and I've lived here for years."
Cllr Majid Mahmood, cabinet member for environment and transport, said: "We know that fly-tipping in Ward End is a concern. We are working in the local area to identify the root cause of the problems and to tackle the issue.
"Fly-tipping harms where we all have to live and work and is carried out by environmental criminals that have no regard for our neighbourhoods or their well-being.
“When fly-tipping occurs, we act as quickly as possible. Our crews clear hundreds of fly-tipping reports each week; this is in addition to the work our neighbourhood crews undertake to clean up across the city.
“Everyone needs to play their part in maintaining a clean environment. We have plenty of lawful options for people to responsibly dispose of waste or unwanted items.
"We are committed to prosecuting fly-tippers whenever possible, and we encourage residents to provide reports and evidence for us to do so."
Delays to waste collection services have been reported by the council today, with problems for bin lorries leaving the Atlas depot on Tuesday morning, as a result of "actions on the picket line".
Birmingham City Council is advising residents to leave rubbish out for collection. They said: "Due to actions on the picket line there are delays in waste wagons leaving our Atlas depot this AM"This may affect the number of collections we are able to make from this depot.
"If today is your collection day, leave  bins out we will collect them asap."
With bin workers on an all-out strike since March, Birmingham has experienced a rise in reports of fly-tipping in recent months.
The industrial action, which has been causing disruption since January this year, has left residents having to endure missed collections and heaps of rubbish in the street.
A recent council performance report has highlighted how the local authority fell short of its fly-tipping and bin collections targets between January 1 and March 31 this year.
It revealed the number of ‘reported missed bin collections per 100,000 collections scheduled’ had missed the quarterly target of 72 – it was instead 960 during this period.
This was also higher than the result of 356 in the third quarter of the year.
Explainer
The report also showed that the percentage of fly-tipping incidents cleared by the street cleansing team within seven calendar days was 73 per cent.
This was one per cent lower compared to the third quarter of the year and failed to meet the council’s quarter target of 95 per cent.
According to a separate report, the strike is estimated to have cost the city council almost £4 million.
In a recent finance report, Birmingham City Council said it incurred a “significant level” of one-off response and clear-up costs during April and May because of the strike.
As the strike continues, additional costs have been building up for agency staff overtime, extended Household Waste and Recycling Centres opening hours, among other expenses.
The council said it was ending negotiations with Unite to resolve the dispute, which was initially triggered by the loss of the Waste Recycling and Collection Officer (WRCO) role.
Striking workers have raised concerns about pay while the Labour-run council’s leadership has repeatedly insisted a “fair and reasonable” offer had been made.

https://www.itv.com/news/central/2025-07.title: Birmingham City Council takes action against union ‘for breaching court order’ over bin strike
https://www.itv.com/news/central/2025-07.text:
Birmingham City Council has applied for contempt of court proceedings against Unite over the long-running bin strike.
The council said it had “persistent evidence” of a breach of a court order previously agreed with Unite.
Union members have been on all-out strike since March in a bitter dispute over pay.
A city council spokesperson said: “We are taking this step to ensure the safety of our city and the safety of our workforce, including those who are on strike.
“Our injunction prevents the blocking of our refuse collection vehicles, both at our depots and on the streets. Despite writing repeatedly to Unite for several weeks to highlight what we believe to be clear breaches of the injunction the situation has worsened.
“Since the injunction was granted, vehicles have been blockaded on roads to and from our depots, with Unite representatives and members stepping in front of, and even leaning against, moving heavy vehicles and blocking road junctions.
“This is dangerous and a serious health and safety risk for the public, the protesters and our workers as well as causing delays to waste collections and to traffic around the city.
“We have said all along that we support the right to peaceful protest and picketing and nothing in our court application today prevents or restricts that or prevents anybody from going on strike.
“The injunction has ordered Unite to ensure all pickets and protests are done safely and lawfully. However nearly every day Unite representatives are blocking roads, slow walking in front of vehicles and abusing our workforce.
“We will now go to court to ensure the safety of all involved and that the terms of the injunction – which has been agreed to by Unite – is adhered to.”
A Unite spokesperson said: “Unite has received notice late today that Birmingham council has applied for contempt of court relating to the injunction which was issued some weeks ago.
"Since then, Unite has worked with our members and reps to ensure that there has been compliance with the court order.
“The court application is the latest distraction from the real task of resolving the ongoing dispute.
"The court papers will be subject to a careful review and the interests of Unite and our members will be fully represented at any future hearing.”

https://www.itv.com/news/calendar/2025-0.title: Protest over ‘devastating’ cuts to transport support for SEND students in Leeds
https://www.itv.com/news/calendar/2025-0.text:
Parents of children with special educational needs say cutting "absolutely essential" school transport funding could have a devastating impact.
From September, SEND students aged over 16 will no longer receive free transport after Leeds City Council decided to axe the service to save £800,000.
Parents say the move will cost them thousands of pounds or force them to cut working hours to drive their children to school.
Campaign group Save Our School Transport gathered outside Leeds Civic Hall on Wednesday ahead of a full council meeting to call for the proposals to be reversed.
Parent Ailith Harley-Roberts said: "These young people have had home-to-school transport since they were probably 11 or before.
"Their needs don't change when they turn 16, but because the council has got to make cuts, they're taking away that home to school transport, which is a vital support for young people and their families.
“These are some of the most vulnerable learners in our city.
“Leeds prides itself on being child-friendly, on being inclusive, and this policy is going to adversely impact on a really vulnerable group of young people and their families who are already struggling.”
'People's needs don't change at 16'
Harry Ward, who has special needs, is now preparing to go to university.
He said: “I went to specialist schools for 11 years and I relied on the school transport system for that time.
“And so seeing this has been devastating for many of the students I know who I went to school with."
Steph Ward, who works for Carers Leeds, has already cut back on working hours to look after her son.
She said: "People's needs don’t change at 16. They're moving into adulthood. For a lot of these young people, people like my son, he will need carers around him for life. Him learning to get on a bus with people, learning to travel with other people - it's a life skill.
“To have that taken away from young people like my son, it's actually setting them back.
"It isn't moving them towards adulthood. It's taking away for some of them the life skills that they need to learn to carry on in their lives.”
Gerry Lavery, of the Unite union, said councillors had failed to "appreciate the significance" of the cuts.
"In a society where it's difficult to have special educational needs and disabilities - to make that position worse - I think puts the young people themselves and the parents and the carers under strain, which is not ideal,” he said.
Leeds City Council has previously said there is no statutory duty to provide transport for post-16 students but it  offered "discretionary assistance" including travel passes, training to help students travel independently and travel allowances.

https://www.itv.com/news/calendar/2025-0.title: Trains cancelled after van collides with level crossing in Knaresborough
https://www.itv.com/news/calendar/2025-0.text:
Trains were disrupted after a van crashed into a level crossing in North Yorkshire.
The vehicle hit a signal box after crashing through the crossing barrier at Knaresborough at about 6.30am on Thursday.
No trains were running between Harrogate and York and services from Leeds towards York were either terminating at Harrogate or were cancelled altogether.
Services from York towards Leeds either started at Harrogate or were cancelled.
The van was removed at 8.30am and normal service resumed at about 11am thanks to "swift repairs", Network Rail said.
A spokesperson said: "It was confirmed that there was no damage to the track itself and temporary fencing was erected to get passengers on the move as soon as possible.
"Network Rail teams will address the remaining damage later, at a time which will cause the least disruption to services."
Nine services were cancelled. Another 25 were affected.
Passengers are still advised to check details of their journey before travelling.
